title: A safe, broadly effective treatment-free cure for chronic hepatitis B

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a safe, finite course of treatment that enables most people with chronic hepatitis B to maintain durable control of the infection after treatment ends. Treatment-free refers to the period after that course: patients would no longer need continuing antiviral suppression to maintain the demonstrated response. Broad effectiveness would require convincing results across clinically relevant patient groups, rather than success confined to a narrowly selected population.

The concept distinguishes functional cure from eradication. Its proposed clinical goal combines sustained suppression of HBV DNA with loss of hepatitis B surface antigen after treatment withdrawal. Achieving that goal would not, by itself, establish that every viral template had been removed. The supplied research identifies persistent viral DNA forms and integrated viral sequences in liver cells as relevant biological obstacles, but the retained source contains no scientific text with which to verify or elaborate those mechanisms. They remain premises of the supplied concept rather than findings established by the available artifact.

significance.text: Conditional significance: a finite, accessible treatment that reliably produces lasting control in most patients would substantially change the treatment burden of chronic hepatitis B. Its direct consequence would be reduced dependence on continuing suppressive medication among those who respond durably. It could also change the frequency or purpose of some treatment-related monitoring, although freedom from medication would not establish freedom from clinical follow-up.

Reductions in liver cancer, liver failure and other long-term complications would be consequential downstream possibilities, but they require separate clinical outcome evidence. Surface-antigen loss and sustained virologic control cannot alone establish the magnitude or timing of those benefits, nor demonstrate that residual risks have disappeared. Accessibility is also a condition of the proposed impact: efficacy in trials would not establish affordability, practical delivery or broad availability.

The useful analogy with an HIV cure is the ambition to achieve durable control after a finite intervention despite persistent infection. That analogy has limits. The supplied concept explicitly avoids treating HBV and HIV reservoirs as biologically identical; a successful strategy, response marker or eradication claim in one infection would not automatically transfer to the other.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a treatment that combines high response rates, durable off-treatment control and acceptable safety across a broad population. These requirements must be achieved together: a response in a minority, control that depends on continued medication, or an intervention with excessive harm would each leave a central part of the proposed innovation unresolved.

Within the biological framing supplied by the research, the scientific challenge is to overcome the consequences of persistent HBV DNA and integrated sequences sufficiently to sustain control after therapy stops. Eradication would impose a further requirement to establish removal or elimination of relevant viral templates. The supplied evidence does not determine whether complete template removal is necessary for durable functional cure, which templates a particular treatment affects, or how reliably any remaining templates can be assessed.

The clinical and engineering challenge includes selecting a finite regimen, determining when treatment can safely stop, detecting relapse and distinguishing durable responses from temporary suppression. Development must also establish how efficacy and harm vary across patient groups, including groups absent or underrepresented in earlier studies. Practical delivery and access would need evaluation alongside biological efficacy. These are synthesis of the proposed capability and its evaluation needs; the retained source does not document their technical resolution.

current_state.text: The supplied research reports two phase 3 trials of bepirovirsen in which 19–20% of treated participants reached the trials’ functional-cure endpoint at week 72, compared with none receiving placebo. It describes selected adults with noncirrhotic disease who were already receiving suppressive therapy and met surface-antigen eligibility limits. It also reports grade 3 or higher adverse events during treatment in 16% versus 3%. The research attributes these results to Hou and colleagues, “Phase 3 Results of Bepirovirsen Treatment for Chronic Hepatitis B Virus Infection,” reportedly published online in the New England Journal of Medicine on 28 May 2026, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2515131. These bibliographic details, numbers, eligibility restrictions and endpoint descriptions are reported assertions that the supplied review could not verify.

The evidence limitation is specific: according to the supplied review, the retained PubMed artifact contains only a cookie interstitial, with no article-identifying content, abstract, trial methods or results. Although the source index records a saved, nontruncated artifact, retention of that page does not establish that the intended article was captured or its identity verified. The earlier research says an abstract was accessible and a journal full-text request returned HTTP 403; neither access assertion is established by the retained material. This prevents confirmation of the reported results and access history; it does not contradict the results or show that they are false.

If confirmed, the reported trial results would represent progress toward functional cure in a selected population. A response rate of 19–20% would still fall well short of the proposed goal of durable control in a large majority. Week-72 assessment alone would not establish years of off-treatment durability without verified information about treatment cessation and subsequent follow-up. The reported adverse-event difference would require fuller information about event types, severity, attribution and clinical consequences before judging acceptable safety. Neither eradication nor reduced liver-cancer or liver-failure outcomes follows from the supplied endpoint description.

The supplied materials contain no bounded search record establishing developments through 1 November 2026. Consequently, they cannot establish whether the reported May 2026 results remained the latest evidence, whether subsequent findings changed their interpretation, or how close the field was to the full proposed capability at that cutoff. This freshness limitation is separate from verification of the dated trial report.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: randomized studies should show that a finite regimen produces confirmed surface-antigen loss and sustained HBV DNA suppression after all relevant suppressive treatment has stopped in a large majority of participants. Protocols should specify the numerical response target, HBV DNA assay and suppression threshold, antigen-loss confirmation procedure, timing of treatment withdrawal and handling of relapse or rescue therapy. These are proposed operational requirements, not established standards supplied by the evidence; no particular numerical definition of “large majority” has been justified here.
completion_criteria.label: Large majority achieve surface-antigen loss and treatment-free HBV DNA suppression

completion_criteria.text: Convincing breadth would require reproducible results across independent studies, sites and diverse populations, including appropriately studied groups underrepresented in earlier trials. Eligibility boundaries and subgroup results should make clear whom the evidence covers. Successful finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, rather than literal effectiveness in every patient or clinical circumstance.
completion_criteria.label: Independent studies reproduce effectiveness across diverse populations within stated boundaries

completion_criteria.text: Durability and safety should be assessed over years of follow-up, with prespecified relapse definitions, adverse-event criteria, monitoring and rescue arrangements. The precise follow-up duration and acceptable risk thresholds remain to be defined and justified. Practical evaluation should also establish whether treatment and any necessary follow-up can be delivered accessibly. A clinical response obtained through a regimen that cannot be safely or feasibly used at scale would satisfy only part of the proposed goal.
completion_criteria.label: Years of follow-up establish durability, safety and accessible delivery

completion_criteria.text: Claims of eradication would require separate evidence addressing residual viral templates and the limits of the measurements used. Claims of reduced liver cancer or liver failure would require long-term outcome studies. Functional cure, eradication and prevention of later liver disease should therefore remain distinct conclusions, each supported by the demonstrations appropriate to it.
completion_criteria.label: Separate evidence supports functional cure, eradication and liver-disease prevention claims

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: INF-02, “A safe, scalable cure for established HIV infection,” is the closest conceptual overlap because both seek durable control of an established viral infection after a finite intervention. HBV and HIV persistence should nevertheless remain separate scientific problems. INF-01, “A broadly protective HIV vaccine,” concerns prevention rather than curing an existing infection.

INF-12, “Very short, reliable curative treatment for active and latent tuberculosis,” shares the goal of shortening treatment while preserving reliable, lasting benefit. Its pathogen, disease states and measures of cure differ from HBV. INF-07, “Broad-spectrum treatment for unrelated viral infections,” instead seeks activity across different viruses; INF-11 seeks broad effectiveness across patients with one infection. Success on either axis would not establish success on the other.

INF-10, “Prevention of multiple sclerosis by controlling Epstein–Barr virus,” and INF-14, “Mechanism-guided prevention of major post-viral syndromes,” overlap with the possibility that controlling infection could prevent later disease. They reinforce the need for separate evidence linking an intervention to downstream outcomes. HBV functional-cure markers cannot establish prevention of liver complications merely by analogy with those concepts.

The remaining roster entries address distinct infectious-disease capabilities: INF-03, INF-08, INF-09 and INF-13 concern vaccination or vaccine response; INF-04 concerns malaria transmission through vectors; INF-05 concerns diagnosis; and INF-06 and INF-15 concern antibacterial treatment platforms. They share broader goals of reducing infectious-disease burden, but none is equivalent to durable off-treatment control of established chronic HBV infection.

unresolved_issues: The intended publication’s identity, bibliographic details and reported trial results remain unverified against scientific content in the supplied artifact.
The exact functional-cure endpoint, treatment-withdrawal schedule, off-treatment follow-up duration, surface-antigen eligibility limits and trial-specific denominators remain unconfirmed.
The reported adverse-event rates require event-level context and attribution before supporting a safety judgment.
The earlier claims of accessible abstract text and a journal full-text HTTP 403 response remain unverified.
Scientific sources supporting the supplied HBV persistence mechanisms and their implications for functional cure versus eradication are absent from the retained material.
The response proportion constituting a large majority, intended population coverage, follow-up duration and acceptable safety criteria remain to be operationally defined.
Evidence for eradication, long-term liver-disease benefits and practical accessibility is not established by the supplied record.
No bounded search record establishes subsequent developments or the field’s position as of 1 November 2026.

brief.title: Lasting hepatitis B control without ongoing medicine
possible: Most people living with chronic hepatitis B could complete a safe course of treatment, then keep the infection controlled without continuing antiviral medicine.
This is called a functional cure: viral DNA, the virus’s genetic material, stays suppressed and surface antigen, a viral coat protein, disappears from blood after treatment stops.
why: People who respond durably could stop taking medicine to suppress the infection. An accessible treatment would reduce the burden of managing chronic hepatitis B.

sources.who: Jinlin Hou and the B-Well Study Group
sources.showed: Bepirovirsen produced functional cure in about one-fifth of treated participants, while placebo produced none. Participants were selected adults without cirrhosis, or advanced liver scarring, already taking antiviral medicine.
sources.quote: In two phase 3 trials involving patients with chronic HBV infection, a functional cure after the discontinuation of NA therapy was reported in significantly more patients treated with bepirovirsen than in those who received placebo.
sources.cited_for: A finite treatment can produce functional cure in some people after antiviral medicine stops.
sources.not_established: The trials do not establish success for most patients, years of durability, or acceptable safety across a broad population.

sources.showed: In a small, partially randomized trial, elebsiran combined with pegylated interferon alfa produced sustained surface-antigen loss in some participants. Follow-up after withdrawal of background antiviral medicine was ongoing.
sources.quote: Elebsiran and PEG-IFNα combination therapy was generally safe and well tolerated.
sources.cited_for: Combination treatment can achieve sustained surface-antigen loss in selected patients.
sources.not_established: Surface-antigen loss after the study treatment does not establish lasting control after all antiviral medicine stops.

sources.showed: The REEF-2 trial combined experimental medicines with standard antivirals before stopping treatment. Surface-antigen levels fell and viral rebound was less frequent, but nobody achieved functional cure.
sources.quote: No patients achieved functional cure at follow-up Week 48.
sources.cited_for: Lower surface-antigen levels and better viral suppression do not necessarily produce functional cure.
sources.not_established: This regimen did not achieve the treatment-free cure being sought.

sources.showed: In liver samples from 16 people with both HIV and hepatitis B, viral DNA embedded in human DNA sustained surface-antigen production in some participants despite antiviral treatment.
sources.quote: We applied a multiplex droplet digital PCR assay to demonstrate that iDNA is responsible for maintaining HBsAg quantities in some individuals.
sources.cited_for: Viral DNA embedded in human DNA can sustain a protein that must disappear for functional cure.
sources.not_established: This small study did not demonstrate a cure or establish whether every remaining viral DNA template must be removed.

shown: Jinlin Hou and the B-Well Study Group achieved functional cure in about one-fifth of participants given bepirovirsen. Eligible participants stopped their background antiviral medicine before the final assessment. Placebo recipients did not achieve functional cure.
That success remains confined to selected patients. More severe adverse events occurred with bepirovirsen than with placebo, and the trials do not establish years of treatment-free control.
missing: A safe, finite treatment that produces lasting control without medicine in a large majority of patients remains to be demonstrated.
Independent studies must establish effectiveness across diverse patient groups.
Years of follow-up must establish durability, safe treatment withdrawal and accessible delivery.
Separate evidence must establish complete virus removal and any reduction in liver cancer or liver failure.

milestones.label: Most patients sustain control after all treatment stops
milestones.explanation: Randomized studies would have to show surface-antigen loss and sustained viral DNA suppression in a large majority after all suppressive treatment stops. This would establish the central treatment-free benefit.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce success across diverse patient groups
milestones.explanation: Independent studies would have to reproduce effectiveness across diverse populations with clear eligibility boundaries. This would establish whom the treatment reliably helps.

milestones.label: Years of follow-up establish safe, accessible, lasting control
milestones.explanation: Follow-up over years would have to establish lasting control, acceptable harms and accessible treatment delivery. This would show whether the benefit can endure and reach patients safely.

milestones.label: Each cure and disease-prevention claim has separate evidence
milestones.explanation: Separate studies would have to support functional cure, complete virus removal and prevention of later liver disease. This would establish which benefits treatment actually delivers.

uncertain: How large a response counts as a large majority, and how long must control last?
Which adverse effects and relapse risks would be acceptable when treatment stops?
Can lasting functional cure leave viral DNA behind, and how reliably can remaining viral DNA be measured?

page.title: Finite treatment for functional cure of chronic hepatitis B
page.definition: A finite regimen gives functional cure to more than half the adults with chronic hepatitis B for whom it is licensed. At 24 weeks after all HBV treatment stops, hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), a viral coat protein, remains undetectable in blood and serum HBV DNA is below 10 IU/mL. Viral DNA can remain in liver cells. The closest licensed regimen, bepirovirsen added to suppressive antiviral therapy, reached its trial endpoint in 19% of treated participants across two pivotal trials, using a DNA cutoff of 20 IU/mL.

goal.need: An estimated 240 million people lived with chronic hepatitis B in 2024. Hepatitis B caused an estimated 1.1 million deaths that year, mostly from cirrhosis and liver cancer. Oral antivirals slow liver damage and reduce liver cancer risk, but they rarely clear the viral surface antigen. Most people who start treatment take it for life. A lasting response would let patients stop taking HBV medication. They would still need follow-up because the infection can flare after treatment stops.

completion.title: A licensed finite HBV regimen produces functional cure in more than half of its intended patients.
completion.criterion: A medicines regulator licenses a finite regimen for adults with chronic HBV infection, supported by pivotal randomized evidence of functional cure in >50% of participants assigned to that regimen in the licensed population. At least 24 weeks after all HBV treatment stops, HBsAg is undetectable with a conventional assay having a detection limit of 0.05 IU/mL and serum HBV DNA is <10 IU/mL; antibodies to HBsAg are optional. The response denominator includes the assigned population, rather than a post hoc responder subgroup. Licensing supplies the benefit–risk judgment. The claim covers only the licensed population.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas: fallback for the majority-response requirement; the individual cure endpoint comes from AASLD–EASL.
completion.basis: Lok proposed HBsAg loss in >50% of patients after a finite course as a research goal. The 2019 EASL–AASLD conference suggested ≥30% HBsAg loss after one year of therapy and called that target arbitrary. The 2022 AASLD–EASL conference defined functional cure for an individual. The Atlas combines that endpoint with a majority of the assigned regimen group and regulatory acceptance of benefit and risk in the licensed population.

milestones.title: An HBV candidate demonstrates antiviral activity in nonclinical testing.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate antiviral activity in cell culture and provide supporting model data appropriate to the candidate. Characterize its mechanism of action, cellular and mitochondrial toxicity, and resistance as applicable. FDA will consider a suitable, validated nonanimal method for equivalence to an animal test. The guidance specifies no universal percentage reduction.

milestones.title: Early human studies establish safety and show antiviral activity in patients with chronic HBV.
milestones.criterion: Early clinical studies provide sufficient safety data and demonstrate antiviral activity in people with chronic HBV to support phase 3 testing. Safety and tolerability can also be assessed in healthy volunteers. FDA specifies no universal response-rate cutoff for this stage.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Chronic Hepatitis B Virus Infection: Developing Drugs for Treatment, section III.A.1.
milestones.threshold_quote: establish safety and evidence of anƟviral acƟvity

milestones.title: A finite HBV regimen produces partial cure 24 weeks after all treatment stops.
milestones.criterion: At 24 weeks after all HBV therapy stops, serum HBsAg remains detectable but below 100 IU/mL, and serum HBV DNA remains below the quantification limit of 10 IU/mL. The clinical benefit of reaching this intermediate HBsAg threshold still requires validation.
milestones.set_by: AASLD–EASL, 2022 HBV-HDV Treatment Endpoints Conference, published in 2023; proposed intermediate endpoint.
milestones.threshold_quote: sustained HBsAg level <100 IU/mL and HBV DNA <LLOQ 24 weeks off-treatment.

milestones.title: A randomized phase 3 trial shows superior off-treatment HBV response with sustained HBsAg loss.
milestones.criterion: The regimen is superior to its prespecified control for sustained HBsAg loss and serum HBV DNA below the assay's quantification limit at the six-month or later off-treatment assessment. All HBV drugs, including any background analogue, must have stopped in responders. In B-Well, eligible patients stop the analogue at week 48 and are assessed at week 72. The protocol limits are 0.05 IU/mL for HBsAg detection and 20 IU/mL for HBV DNA quantification. Rescue treatment precludes response, and the analysis permits isolated blips.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Chronic Hepatitis B Virus Infection: Developing Drugs for Treatment, sections III.B.1.b and III.B.7. B-Well specifies the week-72 implementation.
milestones.threshold_quote: Sustained suppression (6 months or longer) of HBV DNA (less than LLOQ, TD, or TND)

milestones.title: A regulator licenses a finite HBV regimen with rules for stopping background antiviral treatment.
milestones.criterion: A regulator licenses a finite regimen and the label specifies when patients may stop background antiviral therapy. Under the US bepirovirsen label, patients continue the analogue for at least 24 weeks after the bepirovirsen course. Stopping it can then be considered if HBeAg is negative, HBV DNA is <20 IU/mL, HBsAg is undetectable at 0.05 IU/mL, alanine aminotransferase is ≤2 times the upper limit of normal, and the analogue is not needed to treat HIV. The label recommends frequent monitoring for at least one year after withdrawal.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Hibsago prescribing information, sections 1 and 2.7.

milestones.title: A phase 2 trial documents functional cure 24 weeks after all HBV treatment stops.
milestones.criterion: A phase 2 trial documents a participant with sustained HBsAg loss on a conventional assay with a detection limit of 0.05 IU/mL and serum HBV DNA <10 IU/mL at 24 weeks off all HBV therapy. Antibodies to HBsAg are optional. For a participant receiving a background nucleos(t)ide analogue, follow-up off therapy begins when that drug has also stopped.
milestones.set_by: AASLD–EASL, 2022 HBV–HDV Treatment Endpoints Conference, preferred individual endpoint for phase II and III finite-treatment trials.
milestones.threshold_quote: sustained HBsAg loss and HBV DNA less than lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) 24 weeks off-treatment.

not_found: No outside criterion combining cure of most intended patients, numerical population coverage and acceptable safety was found in FDA, NIH or AASLD–EASL documents.

results.finding: B-Well 1 and 2 enrolled 1,834 adults. Across both trials, 19% of participants assigned to bepirovirsen achieved the week 72 off-treatment endpoint.
results.detail: The pooled 19% is calculated from 233 responders among 1,220 participants assigned to bepirovirsen. The placebo arms had zero responders among 614 participants.
results.quote: The percentage of patients with a functional cure at week 72 was significantly higher with bepirovirsen than with placebo both in the B-Well 1 trial (in 127 of 650 patients [20%] vs. none of 328 patients) and in the B-Well 2 trial (in 106 of 570 patients [19%] vs. none of 286 patients).

results.finding: In phase 2 ENSURE, 6 of 18 participants receiving elebsiran 100 mg plus PEG-IFNα had HBsAg loss at week 72.
results.detail: Participants continued background antiviral therapy through week 72. The authors describe ongoing phase 2 studies to address limitations and further validate the findings.

results.quote: Three participants treated with xalnesiran and peg-IFN-alpha were monitored for between 30 and 39 weeks after NA discontinuation, within the temporal requirement of functional cure (≥24 weeks off therapy).

results.finding: After AB-729 and NA withdrawal, 1 of 5 previously NA-suppressed adults met both partial-cure thresholds at week 24 off all therapy.
results.detail: One of the five restarted NA therapy after week 20. In the participant who met both thresholds at week 24, HBV DNA rose to 90 IU/mL by week 36.

case_label = "Baseline treatment status". Reason: Treatment status at trial entry determines whether withdrawal of a background antiviral is needed to demonstrate off-treatment cure.

definition = "A finite regimen gives functional cure to more than half the adults with chronic hepatitis B for whom it is licensed. At 24 weeks after all HBV treatment stops, hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), a viral coat protein, remains undetectable in blood and serum HBV DNA is below 10 IU/mL. Viral DNA can remain in liver cells. The closest licensed regimen, bepirovirsen added to suppressive antiviral therapy, reached its trial endpoint in 19% of treated participants across two pivotal trials, using a DNA cutoff of 20 IU/mL.". Reason: The definition leaves the degree of DNA suppression unspecified and does not distinguish the majority-response goal from the licensed regimen already available.

goal.need = "An estimated 240 million people lived with chronic hepatitis B in 2024. Hepatitis B caused an estimated 1.1 million deaths that year, mostly from cirrhosis and liver cancer. Oral antivirals slow liver damage and reduce liver cancer risk, but they rarely clear the viral surface antigen. Most people who start treatment take it for life. A lasting response would let patients stop taking HBV medication. They would still need follow-up because the infection can flare after treatment stops.". Reason: The current rationale omits what suppressive treatment already does for patients, why it usually continues and why follow-up still matters after withdrawal.

add statement by European Association for the Study of the Liver and American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases, 2019: "The primary endpoint of phase III trials should be functional cure". Reason: The same conference report explicitly identifies functional cure as the primary phase III endpoint.

edit completion: basis = "Lok proposed HBsAg loss in >50% of patients after a finite course as a research goal. The 2019 EASL\u2013AASLD conference suggested \u226530% HBsAg loss after one year of therapy and called that target arbitrary. The 2022 AASLD\u2013EASL conference defined functional cure for an individual. The Atlas combines that endpoint with a majority of the assigned regimen group and regulatory acceptance of benefit and risk in the licensed population."; refs = [3, 4, 5, 20]. Reason: The basis omits a published precedent for the majority target and leaves unclear which elements of the combined test are editorial choices.
add case "Treatment-naive". Reason: AASLD–EASL identify treatment-naive adults as a distinct population for finite-treatment trials.

add case "Suppressed on nucleos(t)ide analogues". Reason: Patients already suppressed on an analogue can retain low HBV DNA while taking it, so their off-treatment results require separate assessment.

edit m1: title = "An HBV candidate demonstrates antiviral activity in nonclinical testing."; criterion = "Demonstrate antiviral activity in cell culture and provide supporting model data appropriate to the candidate. Characterize its mechanism of action, cellular and mitochondrial toxicity, and resistance as applicable. FDA will consider a suitable, validated nonanimal method for equivalence to an animal test. The guidance specifies no universal percentage reduction."; set_by = "FDA, Chronic Hepatitis B Virus Infection: Developing Drugs for Treatment, section III.A.1.b and footnote 9."; threshold_quote = "an\u019fviral ac\u019fvity in cell culture, cytotoxicity, and mitochondrial toxicity"; threshold_ref = 5; refs = [5, 6]. Reason: The criterion embeds a mouse-study result and the title treats animal testing as mandatory despite FDA's provision for equivalent nonanimal methods.

edit m2: title = "Early human studies establish safety and show antiviral activity in patients with chronic HBV."; criterion = "Early clinical studies provide sufficient safety data and demonstrate antiviral activity in people with chronic HBV to support phase 3 testing. FDA specifies no universal response-rate cutoff for this stage."; threshold_quote = "establish safety and evidence of an\u019fviral ac\u019fvity"; threshold_ref = 5. edit m3: criterion = "At 24 weeks after all HBV therapy stops, serum HBsAg remains detectable but below 100 IU/mL, and serum HBV DNA remains below the quantification limit of 10 IU/mL. The clinical benefit of reaching this intermediate HBsAg threshold still requires validation."; threshold_quote = "sustained HBsAg level <100 IU/mL and HBV DNA <LLOQ 24 weeks off-treatment."; threshold_ref = 4. add milestone after m3: "A phase 2 trial documents functional cure 24 weeks after all HBV treatment stops.". Reason: An early trial can document individual functional cures off all therapy before a pivotal trial establishes the treatment effect against a control.

edit m4: title = "A randomized phase 3 trial shows superior off-treatment HBV response with sustained HBsAg loss."; criterion = "The regimen is superior to its prespecified control for sustained HBsAg loss and serum HBV DNA below the assay's quantification limit at the six-month or later off-treatment assessment. All HBV drugs, including any background analogue, must have stopped in responders. In B-Well, eligible patients stop the analogue at week 48 and are assessed at week 72. The protocol limits are 0.05 IU/mL for HBsAg detection and 20 IU/mL for HBV DNA quantification. Rescue treatment precludes response, and the analysis permits isolated blips."; set_by = "FDA, Chronic Hepatitis B Virus Infection: Developing Drugs for Treatment, sections III.B.1.b and III.B.7. Reason: Week 72 is specific to B-Well, while FDA defines the assessment relative to withdrawal of all therapy and allows the comparator to depend on prior treatment.
